#8313. ‘He Looked Like a Moose.’ Missouri Bowhunter Rattled This 221-Inch Buck in to 10 Yards

Published Nov 12, 2026 11:00 AM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

It was cold and rainy the morning of November 6th in northwest Missouri. But the bucks were in rut chasing does, and dedicated bowhunter James Fleener was in his tree saddle long before daylight on a 320-acre hunting lease he has with his brother-in-law.

“I hunted the spot the evening before, and it was ideal,” Fleener tells Outdoor Life. “I knew there was a giant buck in the area. I had lots of trail camera photos of him. I felt good about that place. I left my saddle stand, climbing sticks and bow in the woods that night to return the next morning prepared for an all-day sit.”

Well before daylight he was in a Latitude Outdoors saddle that he used for the first time this year. For him it’s been a hunting game-changer.

“I’d hunted that deer about a dozen times, and moved slowly and quietly into the area where I figured the bucks were pushing does,” says the 26-year-old bowhunter from Lawson, Mo. “I’d hunt a spot, then move 100 yards or so to another place, and get my saddle up in another tree fast and quiet.”

The little maple tree that Fleener hunted from that November 6 morning was near a small pond with a grassy ditch feeding it. That created a natural funnel for deer, and at first light he started seeing does and small bucks.

“I cracked together my rattling antlers and pretty soon a small buck came my way,” he says. “I was watching him come to about 50 yards and I looked beyond him and I saw the big buck through my binoculars about 200 yards off.”

The buck was on the prowl, apparently looking for does. Fleener grunted loudly at the big buck, but he was far off and it was raining so the deer never heard it.

“I grabbed my rattling antlers and cracked them together as loud as I could,” says Fleener, who owns Mid-Mo Trucking Services. “When I did, his head whipped around and he came right to me at a trot. He came fast around a bean field edge. He looked like a moose coming to me at a trot.”

Fleener knew the buck was huge, and looked away for a moment to gather himself, so as not to make a mistake when the deer got in range.

“He was coming right to me and fast, so I drew my bow when he was almost 100 yards away so he wouldn’t see me move to draw,” he says. “At 10 yards he slowed down to cross the grassy ditch, and I let my arrow fly.

“He jumped but never knew what hit him. He moved away at a fast walk, got behind some cover and I thought I heard him crash, but it was wet and rainy, so I wasn’t sure.”

Fleener contacted his good friend Mason Chapman and told him he’d shot a great buck. Chapman was hunting nearby, but he immediately went to help his buddy.

About 30 minutes later Chapman met with Fleener and they tracked the buck, which ran only 40 yards before falling dead.

“When I first saw him up close I was in disbelief,” Fleener says. “This was the first year I’d hunted that lease, and although I knew he was on the property, I had no idea he was really that big.”

Read Next: How to Rattle in a Buck, Based on Whitetail Deer Research

The 14-point whitetail rough scores 221 inches, with an inside spread of about 20 inches. Its rack has a massive palmated antler, with split points on one side.

“I’m going to have a full body mount made of my buck, and I’m still in disbelief about the whole thing.

“I caught the buck in the perfect rut phase, at the right time and place.”

#8310. Winners of the Banff Mountain Film Festival Announced

The annual Banff Centre Mountain Festival gathers mountain luminaries from across the world at the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity in Alberta. There, a celebration of mountain culture recognizes the best outdoor films and books of the past year. The climax of the festival took place this past weekend, and the winners of the 51st annual Banff Mountain Film Competition have now been announced.

The Grand Prize went to Listen, directed by Taliesin Black-Brown. In this short documentary, sound engineer Hank Lentfer records the sounds of nature around his Alaska home, while caring for his mother with dementia. As Lentfer documents the degradation of the natural world, we witness the slow loss of his mother. Drawing together these two threads, the film explores connection despite, and through, loss, using sound.

Rose Bush, an Oscar Award-winning director of photography serving on the competition’s jury, called Listen “a film that engages human-caused environmental devastation — the existential dilemma of our time — at its nucleus with overwhelming love and hope.”

The film also won the Grand Jury Prize at the Tribeca Film Festival.

In addition to a grand prize, the festival honors films in several categories. The winning film in the Adventure category was The Navigator, a feature-length work from director Jordan Manley. The film follows Nainoa Thompson, who was the first Native Hawaiian in six centuries to make the journey from Hawaii to Tahiti in a traditional voyaging canoe. Now, almost five decades later, Thompson and his crew make the journey again, using only traditional navigation techniques.

The best film in the Mountain Culture category was Land of Canaan, produced and directed by Maggie Lemere. Lemere’s film follows a group of Palestinian olive farmers, who work to protect their ancient olive groves amid the destruction by Israel. The film “illuminated the vital relationship of courage, vision, hope, and traditional ecological knowledge,” juror Rose Bush said, “in service of the essential value of sovereignty via mountain culture.”

In the Environment category, director James Dawson’s winning comedic documentary Derek vs Derek follows two Devon farmers, both named Derek. One Derek is an ardent dairy farmer while his environmentalist neighbor begins rewilding his land. A feud naturally ensues.

The Arc’teryx-sponsored Best Climbing Film was Zindabad, directed by Tom Fish. Fish follows Pakistani climber Mueez Ud Din into the Karakoram, alongside his uncle Javed Ali and French climber Mathieu Maynadier. Ud Din explores a remote, unknown glacier system, while the film examines what it means to be a Pakistani climber among peaks long claimed by international outsiders.

Directed by Alexis Berg, the Mountain Sports winner, Roots, follows trail runner Ruth Croft as she examines her future as an elite ultra-trail runner after an injury. Roots is “about an inner journey of healing and acceptance, rooted in the essential joy of running outdoors,” explained juror David Arnaud.

The Snow Sports winner centers on American skier Jessie Diggins. Diggins is the most decorated American cross-country skier ever, but Threshold, directed by Torsten Brinkema, reveals the deep personal struggles behind that success. Juror Beki Henderson noted that “the jury particularly commends Jessie Diggins for her extraordinary courage and honesty in sharing her story.”

There were more mountain films this year than you can even imagine. With 610 film submissions and 83 finalists, it’s no wonder that there are still more category winners.

Best short film winner Hello, Beautiful follows climber Alannah Yip as she struggles with identity, training for the Olympics while enduring medical hair loss. Director Darcy Hennessey created a film which “reminds us that personal transformation does not always come from pushing harder,” juror Kerry Stauffer explained.

For best feature film, the competition announced Ceremony, directed and produced by Banchi Hanuse. The film tells the story of the disappearance of the ooligan, a small fish, from British Columbia’s Bella Coola River. Jurors praised the film’s use of watercolor animation, personal stories, and community broadcasts to explore the importance of a seemingly unimportant little fish.

Director Marco Tribelhorn’s 75 seconds won the Creative Excellence Award. The film documents free-skier Jacob Wester’s 75-second-long battle for survival while trapped in an avalanche.

“A compelling visual treatment brings to life an experience that is impossible to imagine,” said Kerry Stauffer.

Last but not least, the Audience Choice Award went to Only Music // Snake River. Director Justin Fountain’s documentary follows a band that ditches the tour bus for a journey down the Snake River, seeking connection with strangers.

Tickets for the international film festival are now available. We have also covered the recently announced Banff Mountain Book Award winners.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8309. Welcome to the Outdoor Life Shop: Your New Destination for the Best Hunting, Fishing, and Camping Gear

Published Nov 12, 2026 1:14 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Since our very first issue published in 1898, Outdoor Life has covered outdoor gear with independence and rigor. From Jack O’Connor’s old gun columns to today’s in-depth video reviews, field testing gear and reporting the results has always been part of our publication’s DNA.

Which is why I am excited to now introduce our new online gear shop, which represents the culmination of more than a century of gear coverage. This new online retail site will carry a wide variety of quality outdoor products, and purchases made from the site will help to power the Outdoor Life you know and love into the future. There are a few key points that longtime OL readers should know.

If you’ve followed Outdoor Life closely, you know that we’re not scared to piss off folks on occasion. This often includes manufacturers who have overhyped their products. That’s because we believe that reader trust is OL’s single most important asset. If we report the truth, good or bad, we have faith that you will keep coming back. This has been the promise that the OL editors made at the very beginning, and it’s the contract we uphold today.

In all of our gear reviews and buying guides, we will continue to celebrate the top-performing products (whether they are carried in the Outdoor Life shop or not). Likewise, if a product falls short, we’ll continue to call out those flaws.

Unlike some other media outlets in our space, we have no editorial obligation to a single brand. We shoot, hunt with, and wear whatever is new and noteworthy, because that makes the most interesting content. This will continue, regardless of which brands are carried in the shop. Simply scan a few of our recent gear reviews (like our rifle scope test or binocular test) and you will find this to be true.

Over time, the shop will begin to host content from the hundreds of gear reviews we’ve written through the years. Beyond basic specs and product descriptions, the Outdoor Life shop will include details about how the products actually performed during testing. Our “editor’s picks” will highlight the top performing items in a category. Video reviews will show how products work (or don’t work) in the field.

Our aim will be to educate the reader, or potential customer, about the gear they are considering buying, whether they end up buying it from us or someone else.

The OL team is proud that we already spend a ton of time and effort producing the most in-depth gun and gear reviews in the outdoor space. We have been able to fund these efforts by linking to online retailers who sell the gear that we cover. If one of our readers purchases a product from these online retailers, we made a small commission. Added up over the course of the year, these commissions become a meaningful source of revenue that powers our editorial team to create more content.

At its best, it’s a system of meritocracy. Those who create the best content grow the biggest audiences and, in turn, make the most money — to make more content.

But that system has been corrupted with the popularization of Artificial Intelligence. Now, more and more folks are simply asking ChatGPT or Claude, “what’s the best wader for duck hunting?” These chatbots scrape online articles to produce an answer for the user, who then makes their purchase. That hunter will rarely see the original source material. In other words they will never come to our reviews and field tests at Outdoor Life.

And the chatbots don’t much care if they are lifting content from OutdoorLife.com or someone’s basement blog, or even a manufacturer’s own website. In time, this will lead to the degradation (I believe the modern term is “enshittification”) of  gear reviews, and, well, first-hand expert information in general.

Our way to combat this is to own the online shop ourselves. We believe that so long as we have the best and most thorough information, and the best available products, the reader will end up with us.

In the weeks and months to come, we will be adding many more brands and gear categories to the shop. We’ll be offering deals on select products that have performed admirably in our field testing. And we’ll be turning out a lot more stories and videos.

If you’re looking to purchase some new gear, I do hope you check out the OL shop. But the truth is, there are many reasons to love the outdoors and our passion for quality gear is only a sliver of Outdoor Life.  So, after all these years, thank you for reading, following, and watching.

Alex Robinson is Outdoor Life’s editor-in-chief. He oversees an ace team of writers, photographers, and editors who are scattered across the continent and cover everything from backcountry sheep hunting to trail running.

#8306. A 3,300Km Walk Across Japan in Winter

Japanese publisher Katsunari Tanaka has set himself the challenge of hauling a handcart 3,345km from Japan’s northernmost tip to the southern edge of Okinawa in winter.

Tanaka, 49, set off from Cape Sōya in Hokkaido on October 7 and is heading south to Cape Hedo in Okinawa. He hopes to complete the traverse in 100 days over five months. As he will have to contend with some challenging winter conditions along the way, he has described it as “playing chase with winter.”

Rather than carrying everything on his back, he is pulling a handcart that weighs around 100kg. He also has a support team with a vehicle in case of emergencies. At some points, different members of his team have walked with him for a day or so. His daily target is around 35km, with rest days and organized stops built into the schedule.

The first few weeks have already brought strong headwinds, rain, and some steep climbs, making progress difficult at times. Temperatures have dropped close to freezing. At the end of October, he crossed a mountain pass between Yoichi and Iwanai. There, headwinds stirred up the gravel as he walked. Then the snow began. In the end, he took refuge with his support team until the weather improved.

Despite the conditions, Tanaka reached Hakodate Harbor on November 3, having covered 621km across Hokkaido. From Hakodate, he is crossing the Tsugaru Strait by ferry to Aomori, then will continue south along the Sanriku coast to Sendai.

From there, he follows the Pacific coast through Fukushima to Tokyo before joining the Tokaido route toward Osaka before heading west to Kyushu. A second ferry crossing brings him to Okinawa, where he will walk to his final destination, Cape Hedo.

Along a road in Hokkaido. Photo: Katsunari Tanaka/Instagram

This is not Tanaka’s first experience of traveling Japan with a handcart. Around a decade ago, he spent three years visiting all 47 prefectures, selling books directly to people he met along the way. Loading his publications onto a cart, he covered the country between 2013 and 2016, eventually selling 13,477 books. At the time, many people questioned what he was doing and whether books could really be sold on the street. But he says the experience shaped his approach to business and his belief in the power of personal connections.

Tanaka insists that he is not an adventurer. Instead, he is traveling the country as a “merchant.” This time, he is making the journey to support his mentor, Arthur Hollands, a Japanese evangelist known for undertaking lengthy walks while carrying a large wooden cross. Along the route, Tanaka plans to stop at 11 locations to give lectures. He welcomes people to join him for sections of the walk.

Rebecca McPhee is a freelance writer for ExplorersWeb.

Rebecca has been writing about open water sports, adventure travel, and marine science for three years. Prior to that, Rebecca worked as an Editorial Assistant at Taylor and Francis, and a Wildlife Officer for ORCA.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.

#8305. Long Day and Disgusting Dinner — John Muir Trail Day 18

I slept through the night.  OK, I got up to pee several times.

Maybe an apology is in order.  I write a lot about my bodily processes.  Yet on the trail you think about your legs – are they tired or strong;  your lungs – are you gasping for air or breathing clearly and steadily;  your stomach – are you hungry, or do you need a snack;  your feet – are they blistered and hot or cool and comfortable;  your back – is the pack sitting right, or is it aching;  and yes, your bladder, is it full or empty, is your urine a light yellow or is it dark and concerning.

The answers to these questions, and what you do about those answers, determine what your experience is on the trail.  That is the mental element, which is no doubt the most critical of all.  How do you respond to keep the whole organism moving forward successfully?  When do you need to stop and rest, or drink, or eat?  When do you need to push on through pain or discomfort?  So, let me run through the mental process of feeling the need to pee in the middle of the night.

First of all, you’re warm and toasty in your sleeping bag.  You don’t want to leave it for the cold night air outside your tent.

You decide, “I don’t really have to go very badly, let me wait awhile.  No point getting cold just to void a half a bladder, right?”

At a certain point you can’t fall back to sleep and your bladder says to you, “Don’t be an idiot.  You’ve got to go, so go.”

Reluctantly, but a little urgently, you unzip your sleeping bag and pull yourself out.  Then you unzip the tent flap and stick your feet in the shoes you have sheltered in the vestibule.

Then off you go to whatever tree you have designated to fertilize on this particular night.

When you are done, it is a relief.  You are so glad you roused yourself.

Then you look up.  Perhaps the stars are splashed in an ethereal glow across the inky sky?  Perhaps the moon is blasting the mountaintops in a bluish light?  In either case, you are doubly glad you roused yourself, and you pause before returning to your tent.

(Or course, if it is raining, you hightail it back into the tent as fast as you can!)

Back in the tent, your bladder feels empty and your heart feels full.  You fall back to sleep.

I would add that this is the routine for a man.  I recognize that for a woman it is harder and, if she is experiencing her period, it may be much, much harder.  I acknowledge that.

But even when I’m feeling reasonably efficient, I’m just not.  So, getting up at 6:30  means I start hiking at 8:30.  I’m not proud of it, but if I haven’t fixed it by Day 18, it seems unlikely I will at all.

As a result, Ninja Queen left ahead me along with others camping in the area.

After digging – and using — a new cat hole and washing my socks, I finished packing and hit the trail.  Without any major passes to cross, I thought I could log pretty big mileage (for me), to leave a short stretch into Red’s Meadow the next day.  That would be my last resupply.

Immediately the trail went downhill, and I realized it was going to drop down about a thousand feet.  At the bottom was a beautiful mountain stream, splashing gaily over the rocks as it descended.

This was Fish Creek. I didn’t see any fish, but it was a delightful stream.

I also took a video of it and then began an ascent back another thousand feet.

No, I was not climbing a pass, but it was a considerable uphill slog.  Most of it was on an exposed hillside traversing on switchbacks.  I certainly appreciated the traverses!  It would be so much harder without them.

Eventually I caught up to Ninja Queen and we chatted briefly.  Then I passed her, because I’m quite a bit faster than she is on the uphill, probably because she carries such a heavy pack.

Frankly, I feel slow on the uphill, but the discipline of my walking-and-breathing technique maintains my momentum.  By the time I reached the ridge line I was breathing hard, convinced that this was basically a pass, just not a named pass like other more famous ones.

The good news, according to the FarOut app, was that I had completed fully half of the day’s ascent profile, and it was still just mid-morning.

Below the ridge, the trail dropped into a shallow valley where there was a stunning lake with a dark blue color to it.  Lake Virgnia seemed a scenic spot to break for my early snack.  As I sat and nibbled, I watched a person ahead of me follow the trail across the base of the lake.  They seemed to have a problem at a certain point, but they were too far away for me to tell what it was.

Back on the trail, I found the first stream entering the lake to be an easy crossing with steppingstones.

At the second crossing I discovered what the problem was – there were no steppingstones.  Seeing no other option, I dropped my pack.  It annoyed me, because I had just stopped for lunch, and now I had to stop and take everything off all over again to put my water shoes on.  But I did not want to hike in wet shoes and let them squish as I walked until they dried on my feet.

As I waded, the water felt nice and cool on my feet, but the bottom felt sort of muddy and slimy.  I was glad not to be in bare feet.

Once on the other side, I put my shoes and socks back on.  About the time I was ready to go, Ninja Queen had caught up and was facing the same crossing dilemma, except that she didn’t have water shoes.  So, she went through in her bare feet.

I greeted her and refrained from asking if her feet were slimy. Then I set off up the little hill behind the lake and down the other side.  It felt like it was going to be a long day.

From there, there was a long descent to a lake called Purple Lake.  I thought, “Oh, if I only had time, I’d swim in it, because I like the name Purple Lake.”  Purple is, after all, my favorite color.

…and very clear water. If I had the time, it would have been a great swimming spot!

Instead, I just refilled my water bottles there and no, the water wasn’t purple!  But there was a climb above Purple Lake and quite long dry stretch, so I was glad to have the water.

I didn’t have my second lunch until the next stream crossing that I encountered.  It was about 3:00 p.m. and by then I was hot and utterly exhausted.  Some folks I met at the stream, coming the other way, warned me that there was no more water for the next five and a half miles.

So, I filled everything up with water again, but I felt like my legs could barely even move.  I was lethargic and the extra water weight seemed onerous.  I wondered how much further I could go.

Then the calories and nutrition from the lunch kicked in.  My attitude changed completely.  I started going pretty fast and, after another small ascent, the path was smooth and level.  These were ideal conditions for me to make really good time.

I said there were not many views here, but some of them were outstanding!

I just put my head down and hiked and hiked.  There were not many views on this stretch, so there was not a lot of temptation to stop and look around.  At one point though, I finally got a picture of a little chipmunk.

Usually they dashed off too fast, but this one was standing on a rock, and I slowly took out my phone camera, waited until the moment was right, and took some pictures.

There were always so many rodents.  I saw them all the time.  Chipmunks and squirrels and ground squirrels and probably others that I misidentified.

At VVR, one of them even attacked Amy’s granola.  She left it unattended for 10 seconds.  Then there was a chipmunk or a squirrel munching away at it!  (Can’t remember which it was.)  Amy’s response was funny.  She said, “Oh, I got that out of the hiker box, and I didn’t really like it.  So, it’s okay.”

As promised, there was no water for five and a half miles and then there was a stream.  When I was so exhausted before, I intended to stop at the first tent site after the next water source, but now I was ready to continue.

I thought, “Let me fulfill my original plan and get closer to Red’s Meadow.”  I scratched a note in the ground for Ninja Queen, saying that I was going on, but I did not see her again that day.

I pressed on and on.  At one point I found a hat on the trail.  I wondered who — the owner?  someone else? — would pick it up.

Does the rock suggest a deliberate effort to prevent it from blowing away?

At length it was late afternoon, getting towards dusk.  I thought, “Why don’t I just continue and go all the way to Red’s Meadow tonight?  I could pitch my tent, and it could stay in place for two nights, and I would have a true Zero at Red’s Meadow.  It might be wonderful.”

“What is more, it is a full moon, or near a full moon, right now tonight.  It would be easy to see my way, without relying entirely on my headlamp.”

I seemed it was only a little more than four miles further on.

Why didn’t I do that?  What made the difference was a check of the elevation profile.  I saw that Red’s Meadow was more than a thousand feet below where I was then standing.  I thought to myself, “If the descent is a treacherous, rocky downhill hike, and I’m doing it by the moon or by my headlamp, and something happens, no one’s coming.”

During the day, if you had an accident on the trail, another hiker would be sure to come along within an hour, or maybe 90 minutes, tops.  But if that accident happened in the middle of the night?  You would most likely be found the next morning.

Late afternnon on the flat and sandy trail

At the next camping place I saw, up on the hillside above the trail, I pulled off and called it a day.  I had still done almost 19 miles; it was my longest distance yet on the trail.

Up on top there were several camping spots, but I was blissfully alone.  There was little light left, so I quickly set up my tent and began soaking my food.  The freeze dried “Beef in Marinara Sauce” seemed to have congealed inside the package, making me suspicious of the packaging process.  This was my last dinner before resupply and it had a ton of calories, but it was quite disgusting.

Even after I added water, used my utensils to try to break it up, and shook it vigorously in the Nalgene, it remained a semi-solid mass with globules floating around it.

I was worried that I might get food poisoning.  On the other hand, it was my last meal before resupply, I had completed a really long day, and I needed to take in those calories.

I took my chances and began to eat it.  It tasted as terrible as it looked.  Like a prisoner forced to eat his gruel, I forced myself to get it down.  This was my third bad meal on trail, and it moved into first place in the “Worst Meals” competition.

On FarOut, it said that there was a Verizon signal near Red’s Meadow.  I tried it and, to my surprise and delight, I got my wife.  While I waited to begin puking or having diarrhea or something, we had a lovely conversation.

By the time we hung up I was reasonably sure the “dinner” was going to stay down.  I set up my electronics to charge off the block in my tent and snuggled into my sleeping bag.

#8304. Video: The Ultimate Squirrel Rifle

Published Nov 12, 2026 3:00 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

Some people dream of assembling a long-range rifle capable of ringing one-MOA targets at 1,000 yards. Others dream of an ultralight mountain rifle that’s easy to carry for miles and can make a single precision shot. I dream of an ultra-quiet, accurate, and handy rifle for dropping squirrels out of trees. Here’s how I turned a CZ 457 into my dream gun and how it performed in my testing this fall.

The base rifle for this build is a CZ 457 American. I kept the American’s stock because I love a wood stock on a hunting rifle, and its ergonomics work great for squirrel hunting. There are a ton of ultralight chassis you can go with, but wood and squirrel hunting just go together. I did have to sand down the inside of the stock to create room for the new barrel, but that’s easy to do with a palm sander, a dowel wrapped in sandpaper, or every garage gunsmith’s favorite tool: a Dremel.

Lilja makes CZ 457 pre-fit barrels that are fantastic for competition shooting, but I wanted something lighter. That’s why I went with a 16-inch Proof Research pre-fit barrel. One of the great things about the CZ 457 is that the barrel changes are a piece of cake. You simply loosen two set screws to remove the barrel and the new one slides right into the action.

The entire Nightforce NX6 line is fantastic, and the 2-12x F1 variant is perfect for a versatile rimfire. It can take a 50-yard head shot on a squirrel or snap shoot one up close. It also makes this rifle excellent for shooting long range. Dialing in to 300 yards and ringing steel is quite easy with this setup. The scope is fairly light and short, so I don’t think I’m giving up much in terms of weight compared to a traditional 3-9x, but I’m gaining a lot of capability and versatility.

This suppressor is quiet, light, relatively affordable, and easy to clean — everything I look for in a .22 can. There are plenty of other great options like the Dead Air RXD22Ti and the CAT BEN 22 Ti. A .22 silencer is a must-have accessory because it makes shooting a rimfire significantly more fun.

I added an Area 419 CZ 457 Scope Base and bolt handle to my 457 action. The rail makes it much easier to mount scopes and adds some elevation, so I can plink with this rifle out to 300 yards. The bolt handle makes running the bolt easier than the stock round one. One final upgrade I’d like to make is the Timney CZ 457 Trigger.

For accuracy testing, I shot SK Rifle Match, Lapua Center X, and CCI Select. I shot five, five-shot groups with each. All three averaged around a 1/2-inch group at 50 yards. I was most impressed by how well this barrel shot CCI Select, which is relatively inexpensive compared to other ammo I shot.

The new barrel is definitely accurate, and it also made this rifle significantly easier to maneuver in the woods. With the rifle slung over my shoulder it was unobtrusive as I weaved my way through thick cover. When I saw a squirrel, the rifle came to my shoulder quickly and was easy to get stable.

The result of this build is a rifle that’s fun to shoot on the range and a joy to carry in the woods. To me, it perfectly blends a nostalgic wood-stock rifle with modern features. Is it a bit extreme for a squirrel gun? You betcha. But I love this rifle all the same.

#8301. First Ski Descent of Meru Central

Tiphaine Duperier and Boris Langenstein of France have notched another Himalayan first ski descent, this time down the southwest face of Meru Central (6,310m) in India’s Garhwal Himalaya. The skiers are still surprised by how lucky they were.

Duperier admitted they started the expedition with low expectations after several projects earlier in the fall all failed.

“Snow conditions had been unforgiving,” she wrote. “We figured there was only a 3-in-10 chance of skiing the southwest face of Meru.”

But when they got there, the mountain was, they added, “generous” with them.

The three-peaked Meru massif, located in the Gangotri Glacier region of the Garhwal Himalaya, lies between Shivling and Thalay Sagar. It has three peaks: 6,660m Meru South, 6,310m Meru Central, and 6,450m Meru North. The ski descent line is in purple. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein

“We spent six days of reconnaissance and three [days] climbing the peak, [thanks to] an unprecedented stroke of luck in finding a way through the icefall and perfect snow in the upper section,” she explained.

The icefall on Meru Central. Photo: Boris Langenstein

The icefall at the base of the peak was indeed one of the most complex passages. The pair climbed a 15m pitch of WI4 and left a safety rope, which they also used to rappel down after the ski descent, Duperier told PlanetMountain.

Otherwise, the pair of regular expedition and skiing partners climbed alpine-style and pretty fast, reaching the summit in less than eight hours. According to their research, they completed the second-ever ascent of the southwest face of Meru, after an Indian team in 2023.

At the summit on Meru Central. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein

The skiers estimate they covered 1,500m on their descent, with some sections reaching 50 °. Snow conditions were good overall, hard but with a good grip.

“We skied like little monkeys on the wires in Rishikesh,” Duperier posted on social media. “It was just incredible, truly beautiful!”

While the climbers rappelled down the icefall onto the glacier below, the ski descent itself had no rappels or interruptions.

Duperier barely had time to return home to France to pick up a Piolet d’Or for the first alpine-style ascent of the Schell Route on the Rupal Face of Nanga Parbat, followed by the first ski descent from the 8,125m summit.

Tiphaine Duperier at the Piolets d’Or ceremony. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

#8298. Arctic Town Kills Dozens of Grizzlies Feeding on Dump

For years, the grizzlies near Inuvik in Canada’s western Arctic relied on a stable source of food — the town dump. Generations of bears grew up feeding there. In 2025, wildlife officials found that over 40 grizzlies regularly visited the dump.

In 2025, before the fence was built, trail cameras captured multiple grizzlies hanging around the dump, looking for food. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories

It was too much. This year, the town built an electric fence around the site, hoping the bears would move on. They didn’t. Some started coming into town looking for food. Others just hung around the fence, searching for a way in.

“They would just do these laps around the dump, and they would just be emaciated, sickly,” said Toby Halle, a Renewable Resources officer based in Inuvik, told the CBC. “They don’t know what to do with themselves. And quite frankly, we don’t know what to do with them.”

Inuvik, population about 3,500, was the first community in that part of the Arctic to try to wean the bears off their dependence on dump food with such a fence, which cost about $700,000. The problem was, the bears had not learned to depend on any other source of food.

“We’ve probably had three to four generations of bears that have been using that landfill,” said local mayor Peter Clarkson. In the end, the town took a drastic solution — but one that was probably unavoidable in the circumstances: They shot 28 bears.

Tragic though this is, officials hope that within the next couple of years, the remaining bears in the area will move on and learn to eat more natural fare.

Many other Arctic towns still have open dumps where bears come to feed. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories

#8297. Rocks, Ridges, and Roads

I continue my trek through Pennsylvania by facing off with rocky vistas, but also smooth gravel roads.

Progress in Pennsylvania has been swift, the trail follows a relatively straight path across Kittatinny Ridge. The rocks are always a threat to slow things down, but I haven’t found it hard to do 20-25 miles a day even with daylight dwindling as the year moves forward. It feels like my last proper week on the trail. After I finish hiking on Saturday I will have just two more days remaining before heading back to Maryland to attempt the 4 state challenge. First things first, I need to get through this week.

Today should be somewhat eventful. I am hoping to squeeze in 25 miles, I will be crossing through a section of especially difficult rocks known as the Knife’s Edge, passing the unique Eckville Shelter, and ending near a popular viewpoint called The Pinnacle. I did well getting to sleep at a reasonable hour last night, helping me to start southbound from the Bake Oven trailhead around 7:30AM after my morning chores. My first thoughts when I got on the trail: “I am going to love hiking this last bit tomorrow!”. The trail was more of a dirt ATV path, flat, troublesome rocks removed, I could hike flat out, which I now really appreciate after the rocky sections that look flat and easy on the map but are a nuisance.

The flat trail was good while it lasted, but after a mile or so it reverted back to the typical Pennsylvania ridge hiking – a narrow, twisting path with mostly small rocks that weren’t bothersome. But then you’d look ahead and see a sea of boulders and think “the trail can’t possibly be routed through that?” And yet, that is exactly where it goes. I must not be too bothered by the rocks because I only hesitated a little when I saw a sign reading “Bear Rock” pointing to an enormous pile of rocks before sighing deeply and making my way to the top. This was no easy climb, there are blue blazes but hikers can still find plenty of ways up, none of them particularly direct.

A few more miles down the trail I came to another rocky section, but this one wasn’t optional. The trail narrowed to effectively nothing, the trail was just to follow the steeply sloped rocks and find a way to the other side. There was a decent view of the valley to the south, though more of my focus was on staying upright. This section is known as the Knife’s Edge. I don’t imagine it compares to the more famous/infamous Knife’s Edge on Katahdin. Scooby, a thru-hiker I encountered earlier in the year seemed to agree based on her comment on FarOut which I am going to shamelessly steal for your entertainment. I apologize for any language readers may find offensive:

Knife’s Edge my biffin’ boppy! The only Knife’s Edge I know is In THE GREAT NORTHERN MAINE BAXTER WILDERNESS. How dare this thin squirrely rock formation disparage the great Northern edge.

View from the AT near the Allentown Hiking Club Shelter.

I swung through the Allentown Hiking Club Shelter to retrieve a package. In a case of déjà vu, Pebbles had become separated from her Z Seat. I am told that it is actually Greasetrap to blame this time around. With the package secured, I continued along the ridge, which made up the first 14 miles of today’s hike.

The ridge continues west, but soon is divided by the Little Schuylkill River, so the Appalachian Trail shifts south to cross the river in Port Clinton. I won’t get there today, instead the trail heads south through the town of Eckville. There is a unique shelter just off the trail. The property was acquired by the National Park Service and turned into a hiker hostel/shelter in cooperation with the Blue Mountain Eagle Climbing Club, which maintains the AT in the area. In addition, Mick Charowsky, spent decades serving as the shelter caretaker. The property has a flushing toilet and a solar shower. I figured it would be worth checking out and getting a bit of water for my journey. I took a few minutes to peruse the logbook, finding a handful of familiar names, and adding my own name to the historic register.

Come with me, seat pad, you are needed up the trail!

Looking across the valley at The Pinnacle.

Looking across the valley at The Pinnacle.

The trail out of Eckville was the best so far in Pennsylvania. It was mostly a graded gravel road. I didn’t mind the gradual climb which lasted almost the entire 5 miles to The Pinnacle. By this point I had decided I would try to camp nearby so I could catch the sunset/sunrise from the overlook. I’d be coming up a few miles short of the 25 I had in mind, but I had space in my next itinerary to scoop those up. I headed straight for the rocks with my pack on and took in the scene. The Pinnacle sits at the leading edge of a ridge that drops sharply down to the valley just ahead of the viewpoint. An abundance of rocks ensure clear views. The only hitch was that the sun would be setting at the exact opposite angle from the rocks, it was the one thing you could really see. I figured it would still be perfect for sunrise tomorrow and set about finding a flat spot. I found plenty, though there were far fewer that weren’t so overcome with rocks that they seemed like they might lead to ancient Rome. I thought I had a decent spot, no rocks were visible, but when it came time to drive my tent stakes it is became clear that I had merely found a spot with about an inch of soil on top of a lifetime supply of rocks. I wiggled the stakes down until they were just about firm enough to hold for the night.

#8294. No Cameras, No Bait. Old-School Tactics Pay Off for Ohio Bowhunter with 190-Class Buck

Published Nov 12, 2026 5:46 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

It was Dave Talbott’s first year hunting a small farm in southeast Ohio. The property, which is owned by a family friend, has rolling hills and steep hardwoods and is scattered with hayfields.

“I never walked the farm until the week just before bow season opened,” says Talbott, who lives in Logan. “I found good deer sign, with lots of buck rubs on trees.”

Talbott didn’t set any trail cameras or bait. Instead, when the season opened, he just walked the woods, scouting and hunting different locations. He used a lightweight tree saddle and climbing sticks to check areas quickly and quietly.

“I sat in six different trees over 12 hunts, moving according to wind and weather conditions,” says the 26-year-old, who works in heavy construction.

On the morning of Nov. 7, he hunted a pinch point where he knew a few does were bedded.

“But I didn’t like the place and started walking the farm again when I climbed down that morning.”

It was the first cold day of autumn, cloudy and with temperatures around 40 degrees. Talbott located a couple of fresh scrapes, and climbed into a nearby tree around 1:30 p.m. to hunt that afternoon. He didn’t see much until about 4:30. That’s when he spotted a big deer headed his way along the field edge.

“I knew he was big, and a shooter, and it all happened very fast.”

When the buck stepped behind some brush 15 yards from Talbott, he drew. The deer stepped into an opening, and Talbott released his arrow.

Talbott saw the deer run about 30 yards and, pouring blood, enter the timber toward a distant hayfield. Then it disappeared over a hill.

“I was shaking uncontrollably when I called my wife, dad, and best friend [Brady Garren] and told them what had happened,” Talbott says. “Dad and Brady got there after sunset to help me look.”

Carrying flashlights, the three men followed a blood trail for about 150 yards. But the trail petered out. Then they heard thrashing in a nearby ravine. Thinking it might be Talbott’s buck, they backed out and called in Triple BC Deer Drone Recovery for assistance.

“They got there with a drone a couple hours later,” says Talbott. “They flew the drone to where we last found blood and in just a minute the buck was found in the ravine, but its head was up.”

They waited an hour and flew the drone again but saw just a slight movement from the buck. An hour later when they flew the drone a third and final time, they saw the buck was dead.

By then, around 11:30 p.m., more friends had arrived and seven people went into the ravine to help haul out Talbott’s huge buck.

“I knew he was a great buck, but I had no idea he was that big until I walked up to him,” Talbott says. “I was beyond ecstatic.”

It was after midnight by the time they field dressed the buck and dragged it 600 yards to the truck. They loaded it and drove to a friend’s cooler.

The next day Talbott’s wife, Alison, took photos before they caped the buck and processed the meat. The buck has 16 points and is an estimated 5.5 years old.

Read Next: Counter Drone Technology Has Come to Deer Hunting and Landowners Are Starting to Fight Back

“My taxidermist says it should score about 190 inches,” says Talbott. “The whole thing is so unreal I can’t explain how I feel. I spent a lot of time there hunting and learning the farm, how to use the wind and where the deer were bedding and scraping … It’s just an incredible experience.”

#8292. Leonard Clark: Explorer, Spy, Liar

Born in 1907, Leonard Francis Clark was an explorer, war hero, and writer who made daring expeditions all over the world before dying mysteriously in Venezuela in 1957.

Today, he isn’t well known, but has this lack of scrutiny been a blessing in disguise for this forgotten explorer’s legacy? His books, filled with adventure and excitement, read like fiction. The more one digs into the forgotten reports and old newspaper articles, the stranger his story, and the more complicated the man.

A Tibetan expedition under Leonard Clark in 1949. Photo: The Marching Wind

The main sources on Leonard Clark are all, well, Leonard Clark. This isn’t necessarily damning, but it is something he shares with most good con artists or cult leaders. The following is a short biography based only on official records, such as draft cards and census data. The first rule of reading historical accounts is that every historical figure is a liar.

Leonard Francis Clark was born in British Columbia, Canada, in January 1907 to two Americans, Maud and Francis Clark. In 1909, they moved back to Maud’s birth state of California, and Francis promptly died.

There are conflicting statements online about which university he attended, but census data shows him living only a few kilometers from the University of California (now the University of California, Berkeley) in 1930, so I’d put my money on that one. He began traveling right out of college, spending three years in Borneo on a hunting trip with his brother, Laurence. By the late 1930s, he was on a National Geographic-funded expedition to the South China Sea.

His article, cryptically titled Among the Big Knot Lois of Hainan, was published in the 1938 September edition. In it, he recounts how he and a small expeditionary force landed in the midst of a deadly cholera epidemic. Relying on hired porters to carry their supplies, Clark and Nicol Smith, another future travel writer, set off into the interior. Soon, malaria and infection laid low most of the team, including, per Clark’s article, Smith.

Again, according to Clark, Smith urged him to take the remaining five porters, the minimum of equipment, and keep going.

Much of the article is dedicated to ethnographic observations, with the typical exoticism and patronizing tone of the era. At one point, Clark noted that the Li people of Hainan reminded him of indigenous Amazonian people and “the men were tall, many six feet.”

A recent study showed that the average height for men in Hainan today is 168.7cm, around 5’6″, and the same study found that average heights had increased over the past century. This is a small nitpick, but he’ll repeat this unlikely claim again in the Amazon. It is worth noting that the “six-foot-tall Indian warrior” was a stock character in contemporary pulp adventure fiction.

There is an interesting contrast between Clark’s account and some of the newspaper reports, especially one from a Virginia paper, which relied on Smith for the story. This article implies Smith did much more than lay around his tent with malaria. Clark’s article claims he was the first white man to enter 47 different villages, while the newspaper says that Smith was the first Westerner to penetrate inland.

There is a third source: the 37-minute silent film compiled from the expedition’s footage and photographs. In it, we briefly see a white man lying under a mosquito net as if ill. But whether this is Smith, Clark — who admits himself to experiencing malaria symptoms on the expedition — or the third westerner on the expedition, one Jack Munroe, the film doesn’t say.

His previous experience in the region led him to return a few years later, this time on behalf of the U.S. Office of Strategic Services (OSS), a precursor to the CIA. His work during the war centered around the China-Burma-India corridor, particularly the Yellow River valley. He was involved in organizing guerrilla activities, building intelligence networks, and navigating the Japanese surrender of Taiwan.

In a later press statement, Clark explained how he had worked with General Dai Li, and that “the Reds had it in for him,” due to the infamously repressive actions Dai Li took against Chinese Communists. Dai Li, whom historian Barbara Tuchman called “China’s combination of Himmler and J. Edgar Hoover,” was killed in a 1946 plane crash. Wide speculation places the blame for this crash on either the Chinese Communist Party or the OSS. This would make things awkward for Clark a few years later.

He continued his government work in the area after the Second World War, sliding right into the developing Cold War. In 1949, Clark led a large, well-funded expedition into Tibet.

It would have gotten him in the history books if Leonard Clark identified a peak higher than Everest. Unfortunately for him, he didn’t. But he certainly proposed that he had, when he claimed that he’d surveyed Amne Machin and found it to be 9,040m high.

Amne Machin is not taller than Everest. Photo: Wikimedia Commons

Clark published his account of the expedition years later, titled The Marching Wind. In it, he wrote with his typical style: daring escapes, stereotypically aggressive natives, and breezy adventure writing. What it did not contain was the data to support his claims.

As soon as he released his first report and measurements, geographers, geologists, and mountaineers pored over them. Bradford Washburn, a cartographer, photographer, and explorer, published a thorough examination of the surveying techniques and questionable results from Clark’s expedition.

A contemporary review in the Alpine Journal, commenting on his photographic evidence, wrote that “anything more unconvincing could hardly be imagined — yet, ostensibly…the mountain was the object of the expedition.” More on that “ostensibly” later. Suffice it to say, Clark’s estimate that Amne Machin could be almost 1,000m taller than Everest was not adopted by geographers at large.

The review concluded that “it can hardly be wondered if mountaineers, whom Mr. Clark rather despises, cannot accept his results.”

Clark blithely remarked that he had “some rather bulky complaints by mountain and other specialists,” but admitted subpar instruments made his results “indecisive.”

A surveying party including Clark, far right, taking observations of Amne Machin. Photo: The Marching Wind

If he doesn’t seem too broken up, it may be because Amne Machin’s height wasn’t the main purpose of his trip. Clark was supported logistically and went on behalf of Ma Bufang, the fiercely anti-communist warlord ruling Qinghai, on the border of Tibet. Anticipating that he could not long hold out against the People’s Liberation Army, Clark proposed that his expedition would map a path of retreat. This would help Ma Bufang’s army cross into Tibet and continue their anti-Communist campaign from the mountains.

Clark envisioned Ma Bufang’s Qinghai, through Tibet, becoming “the bulwark against Red invasion of India.” Clark went on the expedition and did his mapping, but the PLA took Qinghai only months later, and Ma Bufang fled to Hong Kong.

In his introduction to his book, Clark claims that the United States was unaware of his “very slight aid” to Ma Bufang and local anti-Communist guerrilla activities, and he involved himself with the Chinese Nationalist army “as a private American citizen.” If I were to say that I was skeptical of this claim, I would not be the first to do so. But that falls under speculation, so I will say only that I sent a Freedom of Information Act request to the CIA regarding Clark’s work in Tibet. However, the records were not forthcoming.

After returning from the mountains, Clark went to a wedding anniversary celebration in Canton, surrounded by his fellow Allied intelligence members and their set. Things got a little out of hand, and Clark soon found himself in a Cantonese jail with a bullet wound and two manslaughter charges.

Chinese Nationalist soldiers on Clark’s Tibetan expedition. Photo: The Marching Wind

The other two men involved were Harold Harris, an Englishman who died immediately, and Willard Freeman from Massachusetts, who died later from his injuries. Clark also sustained a gunshot wound, but had recovered sufficiently by late November to be moved from hospital to prison.

The three had been drinking together in Freeman’s home when, at about 4 am, servants reported hearing gunshots. Mrs. Maya Freeman entered the room at 10 am to find an odd and grisly scene. Harris, fully clothed, lay dead on Freeman’s bed with three gunshot wounds. Freeman, completely nude, was also lying on the bed, alive with two shots to the abdomen. Clark, in his underwear, was on a second bed, with a single gunshot to the chest. Furniture was overturned, indicating a fight, and all three were covered in scratches. The only weapon found was Clark’s .32 caliber pistol.

Later that month, the Canton District Court denied Clark’s bail request. The court, still trying to determine what exactly happened, focused on the widowed Maya Freeman. Interviewing her for hours, they attempted to make her confess to an affair with Clark. Both of them repeatedly denied it. Clark further denied that he had fired any of the six shots, though he didn’t name the shooter.

Clark’s brother contacted former OSS head General William Donovan, who rallied the State Department. Clark reportedly was concerned that if he wasn’t released before the city fell to the Communists, he would be tortured for information regarding Dai Li and OSS activities. The State Department investigated and, thanks to its intervention, Clark was released.

Clark’s legal troubles were splashed across newspapers worldwide. Photo: The Journal (Caldwell, Ohio) November 24, 1949

What exactly happened in Freeman’s house that night? Was the dispute between the Allied Intelligence men personal, or professional? If the world were ever to find out, it wouldn’t be from Clark. Once freed, Clark returned to California and moved on to his next adventure. It was an ambitious one: Leonard Clark was going to discover the lost city of El Dorado.

He had an old parchment map to the lost city, he claimed, which showed it lay in the upper reaches of Peru. Never mind that it had been pretty well established for over a century that El Dorado was a myth, following the efforts of explorers Alexander von Humboldt and Robert Schomburgk.

Clark’s resulting account, The Rivers Ran East, contains all the genre tropes you would expect from a fictional work in the same setting. Native Amazonians are ferocious cannibals who capture Clark and keep him in a poison snake pit, crocodiles can and must be lassoed (there are no crocodiles in Peru, only caimans, a type of alligator), and there is a beautiful lady explorer, Inez Pokorny, who is secretly part of a London-based international El Dorado-seeking organization. If this organization existed, I have found no trace of it outside of this book.

If I were to list every blatant impossibility in his account, we would be here for days, so I’ll just continue on one particular thread: Leonard Clark seems to have a very loose grasp of which animals are in Peru and how big they are. At one point, he is blinded by a venom-spitting snake. There are three venom-spitting snake species, and none of them are in South America.

His 500-pound (227kg) boars must be peccaries, pig-like animals native to the Americas. The Amazon native white-lipped peccary tops out around 40kg, while the unconfirmed giant peccary still has only been estimated at 50kg. Likewise, his 12m-long pythons must be anacondas, which have a maximum recorded length of eight meters.

Clark claims to have found El Dorado. What he found was a group of Chicham people panning for gold, who traded some of it to Clark and Pokorny. According to his book, Clark traveled under the pretense of investigating botanical medicines, while actually searching for El Dorado.

In fact, as the El Dorado adventures on the page grew more and more ridiculous, I began to wonder if it were not the other way around. Here I have fully entered the realm of speculation. American corporations were, and still are, extremely interested in extracting resources from South America, including pharmaceuticals. In fact, Clark also reported success in this area, claiming to have identified over 60 native medicinals with commercial possibility — as well as Amazonian oil.

In praise of Clark’s work, Baron Wolfenegg, Director of Colonization for the Orient in Peru, accidentally said the quiet part out loud, stating he’d “learned much from this book that will help my work of colonizing this vast jungle.”

On Peru’s Perené River. Photo: The Rivers Ran East

It is practically gauche for explorers to die in their beds, and Clark, who seemed to mold his life to the shape of adventure stories, was no exception. Clark was in Venezuela in 1957, looking, he claimed, for diamond mines. He entered the Amazon basin, never to emerge again.

One history of the OSS offhandedly mentions that Clark died with “two native arrows in his back.” I suspect the explorer’s penchant for sensationalism survived his death. Other contemporary reports describe Clark as having drowned when his canoe overturned.

As I pointed out earlier, most of the information on Clark’s expeditions came from Clark himself. Since he never returned, startlingly little information is available about his death at age 49.

The area around the Orinoco River in Venezuela is, in fact, rich in diamond deposits. Photo: Wikimedia Commons

The line between fact and fiction is notoriously vague in much of the adventure travel genre. Is Herman Melville telling the full truth about his time spent on the island of Nuku Hiva? Did anyone actually complete the “Long Walk” out of a Soviet detention camp, which Slavomir Rawicz falsely claimed as his own tale? How much artistic license and embellishment is acceptable before exploration accounts become outright hoaxes?

I didn’t write this article with the goal of proving Leonard Clark a charlatan. It can hardly be denied that he really was going to these places, at the very least. But there are enough discrepancies and inaccuracies in his accounts to conclude that they should be taken with a grain of salt, and his treasure-hunting pseudo-archaeological tendencies make his anthropological findings, well, questionable.

As a contemporary New Yorker book critic put it, Clark had “the same gift, or weakness, for grandiose verbiage that got Marco Polo in trouble with his fellow Venetians.”

The real story, and one which may never be fully disentangled, lies in why, exactly, Clark was doing his exploring. Somewhere between the romantic adventurer and the cynically colonialist spy using exploration as a guise for the extractive, violent enforcement of Western capitalist hegemony, lies the truth.

“Every explorer has two faces,” Clark wrote in the opening to The Rivers Ran East; “the secret one and the one he shows to the world.”

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8290. Pennine Way Wrap-Up

Although I only completed 120 miles of the Pennine Way’s 268 mile route, I learned so much.  What went wrong; what went right?  To finish up this blog, I thought I’d summarize my experiences and lessons learned for anyone else who might be considering this adventure.

Compared to the major thru-hikes in the US, the Pennine Way sees only 1,500 to 3,500 thru-hikers each year.  On the morning I started, there were only two other people leaving Edale: Owen (aka SST) and Michael.

Over the course of my journey, I crossed paths with others infrequently and briefly.  Some days, I didn’t see another person except at the pub where I had breakfast or dinner.  There is usually a village somewhere along the day’s route.  However, there are some stretches at the beginning and the end where there is nothing for two or three days.  The terrain feels vast and trackless.  If you don’t enjoy time alone, bring someone with you.

That being said, the British people were universally friendly (except the Uber drivers).  There were many times when I was saved by the kindness of strangers.

The trail is boggy and muddy in sections, rocky and treacherous in others.  Total elevation gain is more than Mount Everest.  The wind is incessant and can be powerful.  Although the temperatures stayed between a mild mid-50s to mid-60s, the wind-chill kept me bundled up even on hard climbs.

When the rain comes—and it will come—it can be anything from a light drizzle to a torrential downpour.  It might be both within the same hour.  Most of the trail provides no shelter, manmade or otherwise.  Full rain gear is essential.  A tent that can be pitched in exposed areas in rain and wind will make a big difference.

I trained for this adventure in inclement weather and on technical terrain with steep climbs.  However, the weather was worse than I had experienced and this made the terrain more challenging. Mental toughness in the face of physical hardship is a must.

I’m one of those travelers who tends to make minimal reservations and just goes where opportunity takes me.  This did not work so well for me on the Pennine.  The villages along the route are tiny and services are very limited.  You might hike all day only to find that there is no place to stay.  Campgrounds close due to weather.  Inns in the smallest villages may have less than six rooms.  Many pubs stop serving food after 6:00 pm. Shops may close by 5:00 or 5:30 pm, and don’t open again until 9:00 am.

While the notion of wild camping is romantic, it was also more challenging than I thought.  You have to be far enough away from farms and villages to remain unnoticed.  However, many of the truly remote locations are on windy, barren hilltops or boggy moors.  The mental toll of not knowing where I would end each day, especially when the weather was really bad, began to take a toll after a few days.

In retrospect, I wish I had researched more camping options and committed to reaching those locations.  Knowing that I was going to be some place I could depend on, even if it took a couple extra miles, would have helped me push through.  I think that’s how Michael, and Graeme and Rachel succeeded.  Michael did a lot of wild camping, but he always had a solid idea of where he would stop for the night.

Finding trail markers can be challenging.  Markers can be hidden behind overgrown foliage, barely legible, or missing entirely due to wind and weather.  If multiple trails share the same route, not all the pertinent trails are listed.  Some areas across the moors are completely unmarked, the trail only revealed through the boot prints of earlier walkers.  I used digital maps linked to GPS, a highly-recommended guidebook, and physical ordinance survey maps.  At times, these three sources contradicted each other, and sometimes disagreed with the physical trail markers.

Graeme told me that having a second person to spot the tiny “acorn” markers was a big help.  From my experience, I wandered off trail at least once every day.  Every time I fell, it was because I was trudging across wild terrain trying to find my way back.  I feel fortunate that I wasn’t injured sooner.

The guidebook claimed that there is no reason to bring more than a 12 kilo (26 pound) pack.  I think the book assumes you’re not camping.  My pack was 30.3 pounds without food.  With food, I think I was carrying around 34 pounds.  With the wisdom of hindsight, I would have packed differently.

I wish I had spent the money to buy a lightweight pack in the 45 to 50 liter range, and a lighter sleeping bag, retaining the 20 degree rating.  Together, my pack and sleeping bag came in at nearly 7 pounds, a big chunk of my base weight.

My research indicated that if I packed 5 days of food, it would last me to the end of the trail.  I should have scaled back my packed meals to 2 days.  While accommodations can be hard to find in the villages, food is easier.  The pubs and cafes are frequent enough, and generally close to campgrounds.  “Honesty shops” (little kiosks of food and drink, paid on the honor system) and snack shops are a welcome treat and usually close to the trail.  Hearty snacks like cheese, protein bars and trail mix are good enough when you’ve had either a full breakfast or dinner in a pub.  While the villages don’t have grocery stores, the smaller towns always had at least a convenience store for resupply.

Between a lighter pack and sleeping bag, and less food, I could have easily shaved 5 pounds or more off my total weight.  For me, 27 pounds total weight would be ideal.

Regardless of how gloomy all of the above sounds, I truly enjoyed my time on the Pennine Way.  In fact, I’m already making plans to try again!  I see what went wrong and I’m more confident than ever that the next attempt will be successful.

For more inspiration, I love this video by Fussyphotos.

Round trip airfare from the US cost me around $1,200 about 2 months before departure.  When I was doing my research, that same flight 6 months before departure was around $850.  Book early.

I’ve you’re traveling from the US, an Electronic Travel Authorization (ETA) is required to enter the UK.  It’s good for one year and cost me about $28.

Train fares from London to Edale, booked 30 days in advance, came to $170.  This required multiple transfers across different transit companies.  If you buy your tickets through an app like the Avanti West Coast, all the required tickets are sold as a bundle.  This app was a lifesaver once I was forced off-trail and had to navigate by train for the remainder of my trip.

Bus and train fares from Kirk Yetholm to Edinburgh came to $40.  Bus routes are managed by each local area, so there aren’t any apps.  However, Google maps was accurate on routes and times and always helped me navigate the bus system.  There is no advance ticket purchase, but I was able to tap a card or digital wallet on every bus I rode.  Even the smallest villages and most remote bus routes accepted electronic payment on the bus.

Pre-booking my hotels 6 months early would have also saved me a lot.  The difference between prices 6 months early and 2 months early was about 40 percent.  Keep in mind that changing exchange rates will affect prices.

A cheap hotel in Manchester and close to the train station, cost me $115 per night.  I went straight from Heathrow Airport to Manchester, avoiding an expensive stay in London.

A major chain hotel in Edinburgh, close to the airport, costs me $255 per night.

On the Pennine, the average price I paid for a double room with a private bathroom was $160 per night. Single rooms with a shared bathroom were often available at 20 to 30 percent less.  Double rooms with only 1 guest were offered at a discount over the same room with 2 guests.  If you’re traveling solo, make sure to adjust your reservation criteria on the inn websites.

Campground fees were generally $13 per night, sometimes discounted for Pennine Way walkers. I’ve since learned that this price can be per person.  I wasn’t aware of this since I was alone.

My original plan was to camp for two nights and sleep indoors every third night.  If I had kept to that plan, I estimate the trip would have cost me about $4,168.  This excludes gear and airfare.  Booking six months in advance would have brought this number down.

My actual costs were quite a bit higher since I spent the second half of my trip off-trail shuttling between various towns and cities.  I had additional transportation costs, and higher average lodging and meal costs for the latter half.

For my next attempt at the Pennine, I’m making several changes:

As challenging as it was, I can’t wait to return and try again.  With a bit of luck and a lot more foreknowledge, I’m going to make it all the way to Scotland!
